semantic_anchor: A sensor model learns by guessing, checking its error, tracing responsibility, and adjusting weights. Backward and the update are different jobs.
prompt: Create a crisp, graphic-rich educational infographic on warm ivory paper, wide 16:9, flat vector illustration with generous space and large readable English labels. Title: 'Guess. Check. Trace. Adjust.' Four equal panels in one horizontal row. Panel 1 teal: label '1. Guess', a small blue sensor dial feeding an adjustable prediction machine, with a blue prediction dot. Panel 2 amber: label '2. Check', compare the blue prediction dot against an orange reference dot with a gap between them, label 'loss'. Panel 3 purple: label '3. Trace', a magnifying glass inspecting the machine and a clipboard, label 'backward: gradients'. Panel 4 green: label '4. Adjust', a hand turning the machine's adjustment knob, label 'step: weights'. Connect adjacent panels left to right with simple arrows. A single curved return arrow from panel 4 back to panel 1 below the panels has label 'guess again'. No other arrows. Tiny footer: 'Same sensor readings. Updated weights.' Use the same little machine throughout; gradients are notes, not automatic knob turns. This is a conceptual diagram, not measured data.
acceptance_criteria: Four stages in exactly this order: Guess, Check, Trace, Adjust. Backward produces gradient notes; only step turns the adjustment knob. Return arrow points from Adjust back to Guess. Text is legible. No numerical training results.
prohibited_content: Mermaid syntax, equations, fabricated loss curves, numerical results, token or pet examples, a hand adjusting weights in the backward panel, extra stages, tangled arrows, logos, photorealism.
alt_text: Four stages of sensor-model training: guess a value, compare it with the reference, use backward to trace gradients, and let the optimizer adjust weights before guessing again.

semantic_anchor: TinyRegressor transforms each sensor reading from one input value into twelve hidden values and then one calibrated prediction; the batch keeps the same number of examples.
prompt: Create a clean graphic-rich learning diagram, wide 16:9, warm ivory background, flat vector style, navy text with teal, blue and amber accents. Title 'One reading. Twelve hidden values. One prediction.' Three panels left to right. Left panel teal: one large circle labeled 'reading', caption '1 value'. Middle panel blue: EXACTLY twelve small feature tiles arranged in 3 rows and 4 columns, all inside one rounded container labeled 'hidden features'; each tile has a simple smooth bend, not measured data; caption '12 values, shaped by tanh'. Right panel amber: one large circle labeled 'prediction', caption '1 value'. One arrow from left panel to middle panel, labeled 'Linear(1, 12)'. One arrow from middle panel to right panel, labeled 'Linear(12, 1)'. Beneath the panels, a thin horizontal rule and a simple text-only band labeled 'Batch shapes'. In this band three large text pills are aligned with their corresponding panels and read exactly '[N, 1]', '[N, 12]', '[N, 1]'. Connect the three pills with arrows. Do NOT draw any tables, matrix grids, or extra tiles in the lower band. Footer: 'More features per reading, not more readings.' N means number of readings and stays the same. The only grid anywhere is the three-by-four group of twelve hidden tiles.
acceptance_criteria: Exactly twelve hidden tiles in a 3 by 4 grid. One input and one output. Linear(1, 12) expands feature count, Linear(12, 1) reduces it. Lower band is text only: [N, 1] -> [N, 12] -> [N, 1], with no drawn matrix grids. The role of tanh is a bend, not a change in shape.
prohibited_content: Any tables or matrix grids in the lower band, other hidden widths, extra output circles, a change in N, claims hidden columns are named physical properties, measured values or loss charts, cat or language examples, formulas, Mermaid syntax, logos, tiny unreadable text.
alt_text: One sensor reading becomes twelve hidden values through Linear and tanh, then one prediction. For a batch, the shapes are N by 1, N by 12, and N by 1; the number of readings never changes.

semantic_anchor: The notebook compares a cloned weight before backward, after backward, and after optimizer.step; gradients appear before the weight changes.
prompt: Create a clear three-panel educational infographic, wide 16:9, warm ivory background, flat vector illustration, very large readable English labels. Title: 'Backward writes the notes. Step turns the knob.' Show the SAME blue adjustment knob in each of three panels. Left panel label 'Before backward': knob pointer at two o'clock, clipboard blank. Middle panel label 'After backward': knob pointer at EXACTLY the SAME two o'clock position, purple clipboard now has several simple plus and minus marks, short caption 'gradients ready; weight unchanged'. Right panel label 'After step': knob pointer has moved to three o'clock, a green hand touches the knob, clipboard remains, caption 'optimizer changes the weight'. Arrow from left to middle labeled 'loss.backward()'. Arrow from middle to right labeled 'optimizer.step()'. Bottom note: 'Concept picture. The code measures the actual change.' No numeric scale on the knobs. Align the knobs so comparing the first two identical positions is effortless.
acceptance_criteria: Three panels only. First and second knob pointers match exactly. Third pointer differs. Gradients appear in the middle panel; the optimizer alone adjusts the knob in the last panel. Code labels and English captions are readable.
prohibited_content: A changed weight or hand turning the knob during backward, numeric gradient or weight values, fake experimental measurements, update arrows before step, equations, token examples, Mermaid syntax, logos, decorative small text.
alt_text: The weight stays unchanged when backward fills gradient notes. Only optimizer.step moves the adjustment knob. The first two panels have identical knob positions.
